subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED ECONOMIC DEVASTATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Ten minutes, Mr. Speaker. I am very pleased to finally rise today to speak on Atlantic Canada. I am always pleased to speak on Atlantic Canada because that is what I was elected to come here and do, along with 19 other Atlantic Canada Liberals, one-quarter of them, by the way, making up the Liberal caucus.
I do regret, however, that the tone of my presentation could not be more positive. With the cumulative effect of the events and the happenings that have so adversely affected Atlantic Canada since the beginning of 1989, this is an occasion for concern. It is an occasion for the loyal Opposition to speak. It is an occasion for the Government to listen and to pay attention to this motion. I will read it to you, Mr. Speaker:
That this House condemns the Government for initiating a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada.
Our people are hurting in Atlantic Canada. It is not something to be ignored in the blind hope that it will go
away. It is impossible to hide because it is so enormous that in the end it is bound to come out. Members of Parliament on this side of the House will not allow it to be ignored. We will not allow it to be hidden. Why are Atlantic Canadians hurting? If anybody in this House has to ask that question, I suggest that they are not with it. They have not been with it for some time and they were certainly not with it in the last few months. Asking that question is a little bit like asking Hitler why the Allies invaded Europe in World War II.
Down East one does not have to be a member of the technical priesthood or the bureaucratic brotherhood to know when you are in trouble. If anybody has any doubt, just take a trip to the East and ask a few questions. Ask the Mayor of Summerside, Prince Edward Island. Ask the workers at the National Sea Plant in Lockeport, Nova Scotia. Ask the fisherman in Shippegan, New Brunswick. Ask a plant worker at the FPI fish plant in Port Union which employs 1,200 people on the Bonavista Peninsula that will be shut down for 19 weeks in 1989. Because of the recent announcements and quota cuts, it will be cut down even more in 1990.
The effect of the Wilson Budget is devastating. This is a Budget that makes a mockery of social economic management. It does nothing for jobs and does nothing for the hopes of a brighter tomorrow. That hits Atlantic Canadians hard.
Ask any of the 65,000 registered commercial fishermen in the Atlantic. Ask any of the 30,000 fish plant workers who work in 900 plants in 1,300 communities in Eastern Canada. The future of the fishing industry is bleak. Tougher times than we have had are ahead, due to the quota cuts, European community and French over-fishing and the shrinking cod stocks. Federal scientists have recently recommended the total catch be reduced to a
125.000	tonnes in 1990, down from the 1988 level of
266.000	tonnes. Mr. Speaker, I do not have to tell you, this is going to have a devastatingly negative effect on fishermen, fish plants and the fish plant workers in my riding.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED ECONOMIC DEVASTATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext: Tory mismanagement.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED ECONOMIC DEVASTATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
This morning, we heard that the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) is reported to have said that we do not know what is going on out there. He was

referring to surveillance in the fishery. It was attributed to the Hon. Member from St. John's East (Mr. Reid) but I do not think he would say something like that.
At a time when greater surveillance is needed to ensure the strict fisheries quotas, the Government now, as a result of the Budget, plans to disband the 29 Tracker fleet of aircraft based at Summerside whose job it is to provide more than half the surveillance hours. That is very difficult to understand. If there is still some question, ask someone collecting unemployment insurance. This Government has cut unemployment insurance funding in the last couple of months by $4.2 billion. That is an average of $1,400 per unemployed worker.
Ask a businessman or an entrepreneur who has been working with ACOA. Its budget has been reduced by $60 million per year for seven years despite all the flip-flop and the reprofiling on all the goods and various figures that have been trotted out. Ask a businessman about the new ground rules and limits on expansion and establishment. Ask him about the turnaround time, how that is to be increased.
Ask the Newfoundland Government about regional development agreements in critical areas to the tune of $100 billion which have not been renegotiated. Ask the average working class person. The tax grab of an average of $700 for each family in Canada will be hard on everyone, and in 1991 Newfoundland will face a 21 per cent federal and provincial tax on goods and services at the point of purchase. This is not a pretty picture.
Ask somebody working at the Albright-Wilson phosphorus plant in Long Harbour which is in the riding of the Hon. Member for St. John's West. That plant will shut down in early August this year. This shutdown will affect the 340 employees, many of whom live in my constituency in the Isthmus and the Trinity Bay area. These people will not have jobs and will be unable to collect unemployment insurance because of a ruling by this Government three years ago which precludes them from doing so when they receive a modest severance allowance. This is unfair, unjust and callous.
Ask the residents of Cape Freels in Bonavista Bay who have to drive to get water from a pond in winter in this
Supply
day and age. Ask anyone in some of the towns and communities in my riding that don't yet have water and sewage facilities. Ask the Mayor of Clarenville, with a population of 2,967, who is living day to day in the hope that something will finally happen with the Hibernia project.
Ask the people of Harbour Grace and Conception Bay North who were promised a penitentiary in their area. It was taken away with one fell swoop of the pen in this Budget. Ask the people who are trying desperately to get some assistance to help turn the tourist industry into a viable industry in Newfoundland. Ask them about some of the difficulties they are having.
We are used to hoping. We would not be Newfoundlanders if we did not have good defences against the curve balls of life which have been thrown our way. We do not feel put upon or feel sorry for ourselves. We do not want something for nothing but history, hindsight and bitter experience made for splendid development of solid defence which allows Newfoundlanders to face harsh facts without denying them. This hope is the backbone of our defence and in the long run helps resolve our difficulties.
Newfoundlanders enjoy music. I recall the words of some of our favourite folk songs which point out over and over the Newfoundlanders' capacity to face the most devastating possibilities with humour. What about Hard, Hard, Times. The song points out the excitement of port life in the midst of starvation. A Great Big Sea Hove in Long Beach makes fun of the tidal wave of 1929 along the beach about a gunshot from my home in Bonavista. Tickle Cove Pond relates an exciting experience of a horse falling through the ice in the spring of the year hauling logs over a not-too-frozen pond.
Something positive has to be done and has to be done soon. I am sick and tired of standing in this House, sitting in this seat, and listening to questions across this floor to a Government which I do not believe is as sensitive to the circumstances as it should be. The Government would not even sit through lunch today to hear some of the concerns of Atlantic Canada. I would say the Government is responsible for bringing about a lot of these effects. How can we expect the Government to do something about the situation if it is responsible for it?

The words of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski) were: "Don't worry about it. It's business as usual". I said we did not expect something for nothing. We do expect something for something in return. What we expect is a stop in our downward economic slide and the growing unemployment. We expect an end to the draining of our people to other parts of Canada and we expect to keep our young people, their talents, potential, ideas and energy at home to build our future.
What we are going to give in return are some positive ideas, some of which were heard here today, some ideas that stand a chance of implementation. Ideas such as income supplements to sustain people who are in the worst need now, better job opportunities through programs like Community Futures and other diversifications, an international initiative to bring nations over-fishing to the table with an aim to setting enforceable quotas. Iceland did it, why not Canada?
In conclusion, Atlantic Canada does not want Ottawa to do it for us. We have more self-respect than that. We want to do it ourselves but we want a fair chance, as the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Rideout) said this morning. We want a fair chance and an equitable share of the pie, a share dispensed wisely to support economic growth which will make our hope and the hope of all our children a reality.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Gander-Grand Falls (Mr. Baker), alleging that the Government should be condemned for the policies it has visited on Canada's Atlantic region.

I have listened since early this morning to speeches made by Members opposite on Atlantic Canada. I would like to say that I hope that Atlantic Canadians are watching this debate because what I have heard is a bunch of disgruntled Grits and a few members of the NDP talking about Atlantic Canada in the same way as the Liberals have always talked about Atlantic Canada, about being a bunch of incompetent people who cannot do anything by themselves and need big brother Ottawa to do everything for them.
I have listened carefully to the Hon. Member for Gander-Grand Falls (Mr. Baker) on the fisheries issue. Later on one of my colleagues will set the record straight on the fisheries issue. The Liberals have not changed. They think they have the comer on everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ALLEGED ECONOMIC DEVASTATION IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, the 200-mile limit. Yet these are the very people who are criticizing this Government for having inflicted these measures on Atlantic Canada. The Hon. Member was a Minister in the former Liberal Government. I also listened to the Member from Porte-aux-Porte-St. Barbe this morning. He was a member of the Liberal Government from 1980 to 1984. The Liberals were in power for a long time but it took the people of Canada to put them where they belong, sitting in opposition. It took the Liberals a long time to learn something about Atlantic Canada. Today they criticize this Government for the way we have treated Atlantic Canada. I invite the Liberal Members to take a sober, second look at what they have been saying and faire travailler les meninges, get their little heads to function and recall what they did to Atlantic Canada.
In 1984 one of the reasons that prompted me to enter federal politics was exactly the heritage left by the Liberals who were in power for 16 years and who inflicted upon Atlantic Canada the kinds of problems we encountered then. That is why I entered politics as an Atlantic Canadian. I am from Atlantic Canada. I listened to them this morning. These are the same people who, in 1984, just a few weeks after the people of Canada decided they had had enough of that bunch, attacked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for his economic renewal plan, arguing that it would kill the economy of Atlantic Canada. The Government's economic renewal policy for Atlantic Canada was about entrepreneurship. It was about telling the people to pick themselves up by their bootstraps and do what they can. We said that we are the tool that can help them, but we will not do it for them.
The Liberals have a recipe for everyone. They had a recipe for Atlantic Canada for 20 years, but what was done? Shortly after 1984, when we laid out a policy for economic renewal for the whole of Atlantic Canada, the
May 29, 1989

Liberals were the prophets of doom and gloom and have opposed that plan in every way possible.
When I hear a Liberal talking about regional development at the federal level, I feel-I will not say how it makes me feel. It is awful to hear that coming from those people who devised a regional economic policy that saw 90 per cent of all federal moneys in regional development being spent in Ontario and Quebec, in central Canada.
The Hon. Member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte (Mr. Tobin), who I call "to tete a Papineau de Terre-Neuve, " knows everything and has all the solutions. According to his rhetoric, he can put fish back into the sea. He was a Member of that Government from 1980 to 1984. If the measure of support to Atlantic Canada is in dollars, then I invite Hon. Members to look at the record. If the measure of support and caring for Atlantic Canada by the Liberal Party is dollars, Liberal Members did not care very much. While they were spending money like drunken sailors all across Canada, they ran up by 1984 a Budget deficit of $40 billion. In terms of regional development, all they could spend in Atlantic Canada was an average of about $182 million a year. Today the Liberals have the gall to criticize the Government for having doubled that commitment to Atlantic Canada in the first four years and for proposing in the next five years to increase that by 35 per cent.
If the measure of caring for Atlantic Canada is in dollars, we score much higher than the Grits at any time of the day. The Liberals' record has been to devise policies that were geared for central Canada. I have nothing against the well being of central Canada, in fact I applaud it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in the House to give this speech in support of the motion of the Hon. Member for Gander-Grand Falls (Mr. Baker).
What we are debating is the federal Government's harsh treatment of Atlantic Canada. Since the last federal election, for some reason, the Atlantic region seems to have been earmarked by the Tory Government. Indeed, the Government has initiated a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada.
The Toiy Government has repeatedly declared its support for what it called "sacred trusts", such as universality of social programs, railway transportation, and regional development, only to go back on its word time and time again.
For example, a few weeks ago the Government attempted to convince the people of Canada that regional spending was not being cut, that it was actually increasing. It is completely beyond me how the Government can claim that it is not a budget cut to spread a five-year spending program over seven years. The facts confirm that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will have its $1.05 billion budget stretched over six or seven years. That is a drop of up to 29 per cent in average annual spending. If that is not a cut, I do not know what it is.
The truth is that the Atlantic provinces are already facing a nearly disastrous situation, with the disembowel-ment of VIA Rail and the reduced fishing quotas. Add to that a reduction in ACOA spending, and one has a recipe for a very serious situation indeed.
May 29, 1989

There is also a big question mark surrounding the Tory Government's continued funding of regional development in the rest of Canada. The last Budget clearly indicated that federal spending on regional development will drop to $1 billion a year over the next five years, from a peak of $1.4 billion in the present fiscal year. It just happened that this was an election year.
The Tory agenda is quite clear. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is treating regional development like a yo-yo; the final spending is anybody's guess. All this uncertainty is especially troubling and will likely have very serious repercussions for Atlantic Canada.
The Government is slashing funds for economic development in the Atlantic Canada area-the country's poorest region-in an attempt to help it reduce its budgetary deficit. The Atlantic region should not have to bear the brunt of the Government's spending cuts.
Last April the Council of Maritime Premiers convened to discuss federal-provincial resource development agreements. During this meeting, the Premier of my home province of New Brunswick, the Hon. Frank McKenna stated that if the money were to expire, employees whose jobs are directly dependent on the agreements quite simply will be out of work. The province is obviously not in a financial position to carry its share of the burden as well as the federal Government's share.
Indirectly, hundreds and perhaps even thousands of people who work in reforestation, build fishing boats, and who work on mineral exploration projects, and who perform all the tasks connected with the delivery of resource agreements, will lose their jobs if the federal Government does not commit itself to a sensible development program.
Regional development agreements have been a valuable tool in helping key areas of the Atlantic economy which have potential to lift the region out of economic disparity. The Government must cease its Draconian treatment of Atlantic Canada, and provide the area with the resources that it needs to achieve its full potential.
Another area of the Atlantic economy which has been ravaged by the Tory Government is passenger rail service. The slashing of VIA Rail funding is a clear
Supply
indication that the Government has turned its back on the people of Atlantic Canada.
Sir John A. Macdonald had a national dream. If he could only see what the Party he once led has done to his dream, he would surely roll over in his grave.
The gradual shutting down of Atlantic Canada's transportation infrastructure is an obvious attempt to isolate the region, and virtually ensures that economic disparity will be one of its permanent features.
The dream of a modem and efficient inter-city rail service in Atlantic Canada is gone, probably forever, because of the Government's recklessness. If VIA Rail is shut down, the Tories will have to answer for this hasty action. Atlantic Canadians want VIA Rail retained and expanded. Last year, VIA's Atlantic branch carried more than 230,000 passengers. In the first three months of this year there is a 10 per cent increase in the number of people using the railway.
Without VIA Rail, Atlantic Canada will become more isolated, jobs will disappear, and inadequate highway systems will suffer more wear and tear. The Tory Party will forever be remembered as the Party which shut down Atlantic Canada.
Atlantic Canada's fisheries are in serious trouble because of the Government's ineptitude. Foreign ships are pillaging Canadian fish stocks with the blessing of the federal Government. The simple truth is that the Government has no policy to deal with foreign overfishing. People have lost jobs, and more may yet lose their jobs because of fisheries troubles.
The drop in cod stocks off Atlantic Canada's coast, confirmed by a recent scientific study, has forced a reduction in fishing quotas. The result has been the closing of fish plants in both Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
Yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) urged Spanish Prime Minister, Felipe Gonzalez, to reduce his country's overfishing of cod stocks outside Canada's 320 kilometre limit. It is high time the Prime Minister started telling the Spanish Prime Minister and leaders of the European Community countries to stop overfishing our waters. Since 1986, the federal Government has permitted member nations of the European Economic Community to overfish Canadian waters. When Spain and Portugal joined the European Community, the European Communities Council of Fisheries Ministers

May 29, 1989
Supply
unilaterally set quotas much higher than those set by the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization. This situation has been permitted to prevail by the Government. It must now account for the disaster facing the Canadian fishing industry.
The Government's concentrated attack on Atlantic Canada includes the undermining of transfer payments, which seriously threatens to harm health care and post-secondary education. It includes the Government's withdrawal of contributions to unemployment insurance, which virtually ensures that people in this region will have to depend on the welfare rolls in order to make ends meet. It includes the closing of rural post offices and a whole slew of other mean-spirited initiatives.
In conclusion, Atlantic Canada should not be victimized by the Tory Government's drastic cuts. This region entered Confederation for very specific reasons, and the present Government has no mandate to undermine the nation building which has gone on for more than 100 years.

In the few minutes that remain I want to talk about one unwieldly word, infrastructure. What is infrastructure, and what does it mean in the context of development? A good comparison is to drive down the 401 toward Toronto. The first thing one notices is the quality of the road and its size. As one approaches the city of Toronto, one will notice the expanse of concrete, asphalt and overpasses within the system of transportation that feeds into that city. As one gets closer still, one can see the subway system, the parks, the hospitals, and harbour facilities, as well as the schools and network of public facilities. All of these are financed by government, whether it is federal, provincial or municipal, and together constitute billions of dollars of infrastructure that is publicly financed in this one city.
The same thing is true when one visits other centres like Montreal, Vancouver and, to a lesser degree perhaps, Halifax and some other cities in our country.
The point I am making is that infrastructure, that collection of publicly financed expenditures over a long period which make up the cities, acts as a magnet to attract industries, investment and jobs. The infrastructure that makes up that city attracts people from all over the country.
Even if business does not receive a nickel in specific assistance to locate in a city like Toronto or Montreal, that business is already benefiting from hundreds of thousands of dollars in infrastructure paid for by government.
There is no way a region like Atlantic Canada, particularly the rural portion, can compete with that unless there is a firm commitment from governments, federal, provincial and municipal, to work together to build up our transportation network, our rail system, our roads, our sewer and water, schools and hospitals in order to develop the infrastructure which makes it possible for businesses to locate there. That is what is missing in the policies of the Government. It is a denial of that long-term continuing commitment.
It is a denial of that long-term continuing commitment to Atlantic Canada to enable our economy to compete fundamentally for what is really necessary to attract and hold jobs as well as to hold our economies together. That is why we on this side of the House consider the renewal at the existing level of the ERDAs so important. They are the main lever by which the federal Government

I have had the privilege of hearing him quite a bit in the last 10 days, on radio and television. This gives me a particular opportunity to be able to put some order and some sense

into what I know is real compassion and passion but which unfortunately clouds reality and the facts.
We are talking today about the motion that he has put forward in this House which condemns the Government for initiating a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada. I would argue that the policies of this Government, particularly over the last five years, have done absolutely the opposite. In my province, we have seen a reduction in the unemployment rate of some 8 per cent, the highest reduction in the unemployment rate in any province in this country. Last year alone, we saw the creation of 10,000 jobs in Newfoundland and Labrador. This is an accomplishment that we have never seen before, certainly in the 40 years we have been part of this great country and the 400 years before that.
My colleagues have talked extensively about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and other things. I would like, if I may, to concentrate on the fishery. The lifeblood of Newfoundland and Labrador is and has always been, and I would suggest will always be, the fishery. It brought us to what is now that province. It has kept us there. It has gone through a series of good times and it has gone through a series of bad times.
There is no question that I, and I think all Members in this House, recognize that in the next few years we will have a very difficult time in the fishery in Eastern Canada. It is a very difficult time for all of us, whether we are in the fishery or whatever part of the economy that we are in. The problem is serious. Potentially, the problem is one that we must all work together to find solutions for.
The Harris interim report that was released last Friday has told us that we may face some serious cut-backs in the northern cod stock. It has told us that we have much work to do to be sure of the state of that stock. It has told us that there is much that has to be done over a period of time to ensure that that stock is there. I think that all Members of this House, on whatever side they sit, will agree that the conservation of all our fish stocks must be our first concern because it is the long-term viability of the fishery that is vital to those thousands of people, as my hon. friend from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception has told us, those tens of thousands of people who depend

May 29, 1989
Supply
on the fishery. The solutions to this problem are not going to be found overnight.
The solutions to this problem are only going to be found with much consultation and co-operation from all of the parties that are involved in the fishery, be they fishermen or the union, be they plant workers or people who work on trawlers, or the companies or the provincial Government and the federal Government. It is only working together, recognizing what the problem is and recognizing what the impact of those problems will be, and working together to find solutions that address the fishery, the economy and the social net that we must have to ensure that as many people in Atlantic Canada as possible can work and live in that fishery. It is the policies of this Government that will ensure that we have a viable and strong fishery.
Let us just talk a little bit about where we have been in the last few years. From 1984 to 1987, the value of landings, this is the effect of the Tory policies. The value of landings has increased by 88 per cent. In the ground-fish sector, landed values increased by 93 per cent. In the shellfish sector, landed values increased by 81 per cent. The value of production increased by 75 per cent, to $2.4 billion. In 1987, Atlantic coast production amounted to $2.4 billion, an increase of 15.6 per cent from $2.1 billion in 1986. The value of landings compared to the previous year was up 27 per cent. The value of groundfish was up 41 per cent. I could go into other species but I will not.
I want to speak directly to what my friend from Gander-Grand Falls said this morning. There are two or three things that he referred to that I think demand a response. First, I want to talk about the general problem of overfishing. There is no question that overfishing by foreign countries and fishing by foreign countries have taken fish out of our waters. Let us put it into some context. If we first of all believe that that is the only problem facing our fishery, that that is the only reason we face a reduced total allowable catch perhaps next year or the year after, we are sadly deluding ourselves and all of those who have elected us to represent them.
There are a series of problems, just as there are a series of solutions. We must recognize those problems in reality and then get solutions in terms of reality. The Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Harb) has said that
there has to be co-operation. There has to be a sense of reality. There has to be a sense of proportion here. I think that all of us at the end of the day would like to find that.
The overfishing or foreign fishing in the last two years has reduced dramatically. The catches are down from 1986 of 171,000 tonnes to 66,000 tonnes in 1988. Overfishing is down in somewhat the same proportion.
This Government has taken a whole series of actions to address and attack the problem of overfishing. We recognize it is a problem. It has been going on for years. There have been agreements historically and agreements that have been renegotiated that have gone back over a period of time. There is precedent that we have to deal with. Part of having a 200-mile limit that is respected because of international law and international precedent demands that we do certain things. Part of that is to make available surplus stocks, species that we do not take, to international fisheries and to other countries. We are complying with those obligations. I will go back to that.
In terms of overfishing, we have closed our ports to ships of countries that continue to overfish against their obligations. We refuse allocations inside our zone to those same countries. Surveillance and enforcement along the 200-mile limit has been improved to prevent illegal incursions. Penalties have been increased substantially to provide a deterrent to those captains, those countries, and those fish companies for offshore that want to come in and think that they can abuse our fish stocks.
This Government will continue its efforts to gamer international acceptance of the enhanced coastal state preferential rights with respect to management and conservation of straddling stocks. This is something that there is clearly an opportunity to pursue, and pursue it we will and we are. The statement of this Government, the first Speech from the Throne of this new Government made quite clear its concern and its intention to address overfishing.

speechtext:

The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) will be meeting European counterparts in the coming weeks, and they will make very clear our concern that this practice must stop, not just in the interests of Canadian fishermen but in a time of international acceptance of the premise and the understanding of development and responsible management of the environment, where sustainable development has become a catch word. Management is a critical component of that.
If I may briefly turn to some of the comments made by my friend from Gander-Grand Falls. His constituents welcomed him into that great paper city. I am sure he entertains them as much as he has the people of Gander and parts of the northeast coast of Newfoundland, but unfortunately we are not talking here about entertainment. In fact, it is very unentertaining. It is very serious and is not serving anyone's interest if we continue to use scare tactics, to inflate the situation and make the people of this country insecure based on something that is not there. If we continue to do this, we will get nowhere.
The attitude of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Harb) and what I was hearing from my friend, the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Mifflin) and some others is that we must all recognize the seriousness of this issue.
We talked about the 35 Soviet fish plants and the nine Cuban fish plants due east of St. John's licensed to fish off the coast of Halifax for silver hake bycatches of 3,000
Supply
tonnes of cod, 3,000 tonnes of pollock and 1,000 tonnes of haddock. I stand corrected if I am wrong. Those numbers are not realistic. Those numbers are perhaps the tolerance that are provided for in bycatch. You cannot avoid a bycatch. If we are going to allow these countries to take a species that we are not equipped or not prepared to take, there will be a bycatch. I think it is important to recognize what the bycatches were in 1988. The bycatches for all three of those species for the Soviets were 1,500 tonnes, not the 7,000 tonnes about which the Hon. Member is talking. The bycatches were 1,500 tonnes for all of the species. That is less than .3 per cent of the total fishery. The Hon. Member talks about 250 fish plants floating around out there. This is simply not the case. It is not happening.
The Hon. Member talks about capelin and how others are allowed to take capelin while Newfoundland fishermen are not allowed to. Let us recognize how capelin is licensed in Newfoundland and Labrador. The licensing for capelin and the allowable catches for capelin are based on the market. It is the market that dictates what can be taken, how much is going to be purchased. Therefore, we take what we know will be sold based on female roe capelin. As a result the limits are dictated by that. Capelin are being caught for the fish. It is apples and oranges and any denial of a Newfoundlander for a licence in an attempt to make sure we only catch what we can sell would not be affected by whoever was out there. If no one was out there, it would not change. It would be exactly the same.
Newfoundlanders are charged and fined for incidental catches, but not foreign vessels? There have been foreign vessels fined this year. One Soviet vessel was charged for dumping fish and another was ordered out of the zone for not reporting bycatches.
The Soviets and the Cubans are not coming anywhere near the bycatch levels. In 1988 the haddock limit was 1 per cent. They caught .59 per cent. In 4W where the limit on cod is 5 per cent, the Soviets caught .16 per cent. Of course, they are not charged because they are nowhere near the limits. If we are catching a total 1,500 tonnes of fish out of a total that is being presented to us in terms of
7,000	tonnes, of course, they are not charged. Why are there 250 factory-freezer trawlers inside the 200-mile zone?

We have issued 61 fishing licences. Vessels are issued licences for a number of things such as research or perhaps over-the-side-sales. You need a licence for the different fisheries. It also denies the fact that the quota is not based on the amount of fish a ship catches. The quota is fixed. Fleets are given an amount of fish based on our obligations and are based entirely on a block. They could have 15,000 ships out there and it would not affect the amount of fish caught. Anyone inside the 200-mile limit has a Canadian observer on that ship 100 per cent of the time. This observer reports to the Department of Fisheries so that the Department knows exactly how much fish is being caught.
The policy on allowing people to fish in our waters is very clear. Canada has an obligation under international law to make surplus stocks available to other countries with which it has bilateral fisheries agreements. Examples, as we know, are silver hake, capelin, argentine, grenadier. When and if-this is very important-these fisheries are developed by Canadians then the present foreign effort will be reduced accordingly.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has undertaken a whole series of programs to address the opportunities of underdeveloped species. We know about exploratory licences for crab, clams and scallops. We know about moving further north with exploratory licences for shrimp. We know about the work done for aquaculture. We know about the Icelandic scallop fishery, the offshore clam fishery, the work we have done with native fishermen to try to get them involved in the fishery.
The fishing effort and the landed value has tripled in the last three years. There continues to be movements of allocations so that when the fish are not caught, we are in the position that we can move it to someone else. For instance, in the case of the Soviets where there was a particular type of fish they were unable to catch, we exchanged it for a fish for which we had quotas available that Canadians were not catching. In that case we were able to take cod back. It is that type of innovation, creativity and co-operation why we continue to have growth in the value of our fishery, why our fishermen continue to do well and want to continue in the fishery and why we have confidence in addressing what we recognize as a serious problem. The base is there. The good policy that is being condemned by the Hon. Member is there. It is a policy that will allow us to develop and adapt.
The Prime Minister has appointed a cabinet committee which will address specifically these opportunities and problems to make sure we maximize the fishery and to make sure we use all of the tools available to us to make sure as many people in Atlantic Canada who want to live and work in the fishery in Atlantic Canada know they will have an income that is dependable and will have a strong future for themselves and their communities. Those are the policies which the Opposition want to condemn. Those are the policies that the crowd opposite want to condemn which will ensure that whatever happens in the future, we will have that strong, viable fishery.

I want to thank the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Reid) for his presentation. I found some of the figures very interesting and some of the qualitative descriptions also very interesting.
I would like to make a few comments. First, I would remind the House that it was the Government composed of those of us who are on this side of the House that commissioned the Kirby Commission to put the Atlantic fisheries in a better position than it had been in some time. It was also the Liberal Government that spearheaded the whole business of the change to the 200-mile economic zone in 1977 and organized forces in the Canadian Government to carry out surveillance. Indeed, it was the Liberal Government that set the policy that put us in a pretty good position.
I would like to talk about some of the things that are going on right now. I do not think that there is any question that over the last four or five years, our quotas, for whatever reason, and I am in no position to make any judgment on that, have not been the kind of quotas we should have had. A more serious environmental problem has been the overfishing by the European Community. I will not talk about that now because I think it was covered by the Hon. Member for Gander-Grand Falls (Mr. Baker) this morning.
I want to talk about fishing outside the 200-mile economic zone. I would like to refer to some figures. Last year, the Economic Community's quota in international waters off Newfoundland was 19,000 metric tons, but the European Community ships and craft hauled in
80,000	metric tons, over four times what they were allocated. Quotas in that area are voluntary and set on the basis of scientific information and evidence compiled by the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization,

NAFO, a voluntary group in which Canada and the European Community are members.
This year, 1989, this voluntary organization established a quota of 13,000 tonnes one more time for the Economic Community, but the Economic Community fisheries ministers, prodded by Portugal and Spain, no doubt, responded in December by setting their own quotas of from 13,000 to 160,000 metric tons. We talk about conservation while this sort of thing is going on.
I am sure the Hon. Member and other Hon. Members would say that the Prime Minister is over there talking about this and that he will do something about it. This has been going on for a long time. If we want to do something about it, and if we soon do not reach an accommodation on overfishing, I suggest that we take a look at some trade sanctions. We could direct them to some of the main European Community players.
Let me give Hon. Members an indication of what we could do. I am not sure how easy it will be in the case of Portugal. Portugal had a two-way trade with Canada last year of $286 million. There was a deficit of $48 million, but in the case of Spain which has been brought to the attention of the House this morning, it is certainly the more vulnerable of the two and last year enjoyed a $485 million trade surplus with Canada on the total two-way trade of $945 million. I think we can make use of this in some way, shape or form.
The other point I want to make is that in the last three and a half or four years, the French have been allocated around 6,400 tonnes of northern cod in 3PS, the south of Newfoundland. We have heard a lot about 3PS. The French have been catching four times that, 26,000 tonnes. We negotiated a deal with them so that we can come back to the table in two or three years' time and allocate a quota which is virtually the same amount, not 6,400 tonnes but around 25,000 tonnes while we are waiting for negotiations three years from now.
If we are concerned about conservation, I do not know how we can allow these things to happen without taking advantage of trade sanctions in support of conversation. I

Mr. Speaker, I could not help in listening to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Reid) when he was responding to a question from the Opposition. He was getting quite rattled and said that the Opposition was making people feel insecure, and that we should not be making people in the Atlantic feel insecure. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what makes people feel insecure. It ought to make people, not only in Atlantic Canada, but all Canadians very insecure. I want to put on the record the latest unemployment figures for the various Atlantic provinces unadjusted in April, 1989. The unemployment rate in Prince Edward Island was 17.8 per cent, Newfoundland, 17.2 per cent, Nova Scotia, 12.2 per cent and in New Brunswick, it is 14.4 per cent.
These figures would make anybody insecure. We ought to be ashamed of ourselves. The unemployment rate for 15 to 24 year old males in Newfoundland is 30.5 per cent, in Nova Scotia it is 18.4 per cent, in New Brunswick, it is 28.8 per cent. For women 15 to 24 years old in Newfoundland, it is 20.7 per cent, Nova Scotia, 15.6 per cent and New Brunswick, 14.6 per cent. For P.E.I., the numbers are too small to give a reading.
It is not what the Opposition does or says in this House that creates insecurity in Atlantic Canada. These are the unemployment realities. Yet the Government's full employment rate for all of Canada is somewhere between 7.5 per cent and 8 per cent. That is the Government's vision of full employment in this nation. These figures are not any different than what they were in 1972. Nothing much has changed. We have had Liberals sitting in Government and we have had Tories. When we do not like the Liberals, we put the Tories in. When we do not like the Tories in the Atlantic, we elect Liberals. It is the old story of Tweedle-Dum and Tweedle-Dee. The people of Atlantic Canada put their faith in those they elect. They believe that some change might occur but no changes occur. We just finished the federal election. Before that election was called, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his government stood up and made a promise about Hibernia. That was a spending commitment. It was not like what the New Democrats were saying and what the Liberals were saying. We were making election promises. eastern Canada who is the Minister for International Trade, the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said in October, 1988 that it is just scaremongers in the Opposition. We do not intend to change. The unemployment insurance program will not change one jot or tittle.

You have to say, Atlantic Canada, you are on your own."
Imagine that. After the election, we get the truth, and it is as if Mickey Cohen was not telling all the truth. We get a Government that comes in here and barefacedly attacks the Atlantic region, a region which is much like my own in northern Ontario. It attacks by cutting back regional development spending in the Atlantic, a place
Supply
where there ought to be more spending, not less. As the figures indicate, the problems are far more serious than in Toronto or most other parts of this country.
So what do we have? We have a cut-back in regional development programs. We have a cut-back in unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance was probably the only lifeline between people who become unemployed in the Atlantic and some kind of dignity. At least they are paid premiums. There is dignity collecting on the basis of premiums you have paid while you were working. They are eliminating that by increasing the number of weeks you have to work and cutting back on the number of weeks that you collect. It is no wonder the commission set up to study post-free trade said that what you need is not a net, what you need is a trampoline. Atlantic Canadians are going to be trampolined all the way to Toronto so they can work selling John Bulloch suits and Mary Dosie's shoes for $9 or $6 an hour for a grand total of about $15,000 to $16,000 a year and 60 of them will live in one apartment. So they are living on the edge of poverty in the Atlantic or will be living in dire poverty in Toronto. It is bad enough living in Toronto but then to have to live on those wages as well is a punishment only Tories deserve.
There is no question that this Government, as the motion states, has cut back programs to the Atlantic.
Last week I was in Prince Edward Island, and lo and behold the Government announced that it was closing a base at Summerside. Only an insensitive stockbroker from Bay Street would understand closing the only industry on which 90 per cent of the community of Summerside depends. Not only has this economic activity for the people of Summerside been eliminated in one fell swoop, but it also serves as a tracker station for supervising our 200-mile limit. I am not the only one who has stated that, but also the people in leadership positions locally in Prince Edward Island are asking the Government why it is doing that to them. It is cruel.
We never heard a word about deficit or debt during the campaign. Suddenly, after the election campaign, I am faced with the prospect of my sons and daughters and their children's children for generation after generation having to live with a mortgaged country. I would rather

May 29, 1989
Supply
they lived with a mortgaged country than have to live with rundown hospitals where services cannot be provided. I would rather they lived with a mortgaged country than to have schools that cannot be supportive and cannot provide opportunities for them to earn a living and to live with dignity in their communities. That is the option we have been given. Cut back post-secondary education and cut-back health care. That is it.
Then the Government turns around and spends the taxpayers' money to tell them a pack of lies on television about one-third of the loony being taken to pay for the interest on the debt. The Government takes out one-third of the loony, Mr. Speaker. I think that what we have to do is take the loonies out of the Government over there and put the country straight.

Mr. 'Rimer (Halton-Peel): I found the comments of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) highly interesting, and I think that a couple of points bear some comment.
The Hon. Member is somewhat correct in his statement that during the election campaign the issues of the debt and the deficit were not adequately addressed. It needs to be said that many candidates during the election campaign did want to talk about this situation. I wanted to talk about it, and I know that many colleagues did.
The debt and the deficit have not materialized overnight. They have not come out of thin air. The Hon. Member has been in the House a long time and he knows very well that we have run annual deficits as a matter of course in this country for most of the past 20 years. It did not materialize overnight.
What happened during the election was that the issue of free trade was made by the opposition Parties, particularly the Liberals, as the one and only issue that had to be addressed.
The Hon. Member states that he would rather live in a mortgaged country than have reduced services. Does the Hon. Member not recognize that, at some point living in a mortgaged country, it gets to the point where the mortgage is so large that we cannot make both those mortgage payments plus fund the social services the
Hon. Member is talking about. I agree with the Hon. Member that we need good schools, roads, and hospitals. We need to help regions of the country that are deserving of it, or are down on their luck for one reason or another. Is the Hon. Member not concerned that at some point we will not be able to fund those very programs because we are being shackled and dragged down by the interest payments? How can the Hon. speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I do not know if all of those who here remember the period leading up to the election and the period during the election. In the period leading up to the election, whenever questions were posed about the economy or the health of the economy, government Members took a considerable amount of credit and assured us and Canadians that everything was under control, and that the deficit was in line with the projections of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Everything is under control, have no fear, Mike is here. That was the slogan.
While I agree with the Hon. Member that during the election free trade was the overriding issue, the fact is that any single time the question was put to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Finance during the campaign, we were not told that we had a problem. Everything was under control. Mike is on the bridge. As far as I knew, the Titanic was on course at that time. Somebody moved a giant iceberg in front of the Titanic after November 21, and now they are all arranging the deck seats on the Titanic.
The Hon. Member mentioned the deficit. I would not mind if the Government would at least tell us the truth. Two weeks ago there was an interesting article in one of the newspapers. It was an open statement by approximately 21 Canadian economists, some of whom were very well known. They took the Government to task. Since the Hon. Member is the Chairman of the Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I suggest to him that he ought to look seriously at the fact that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Val-court) should be asked to investigate misleading and false advertising.

In that article I read that the Government is not telling the people the truth about the deficit. In fact, the credit demands of the Crown will only be $20 billion, and another $3 billion for foreign reserve borrowing. Therefore, it is not $28 billion and $29 billion of borrowing that the Government will have to do. The economists presented an entirely different picture that the deficit was quite manageable.
In light of how I commenced my speech today, I say to my friend that the greater emphasis ought to be to ensure that every Canadian who wants to work has a job. There is far greater dignity in people having a job, earning, being productive, paying taxes, buying goods, buying services, and paying municipal, provincial and federal taxes. Those are the types of positive moves, not accepting 7.5 per cent unemployment, but actually moving to zero per cent unemployment, or as close to it as we can get. I think that anything else is regressive. That is why we call the Government the "regressive" Conservatives.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you appreciate that I find myself in the difficult position of following my dear colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), who inspires us all with his analysis of the economic situation in which the Government has cast us. Nevertheless, I will plunge ahead.
Today we are dealing with the Liberal motion which states:
That this House condemns the Government for initiating a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada.
I would only change the motion in one respect, and that is: "That this House condemns the Government for continuing a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada". What we have here is only a continuation of the same old song. The silent song that is sung to earn votes, but not after all to bring any substantial change to the situation in Atlantic Canada which would make itself sustaining and
Supply
equal in the confederation to the core of Canada which seems otherwise so blessed.
It is absolutely astounding to me that the experience we had two weeks ago when the Minister responsible for ACOA came to our committee and without any warning announced that the funding for ACOA would be stretched over seven years rather than five years, thus imposing essentially a 28 per cent cut in the annual rate of expenditures to that program. That has to be seen as a devastating attack and a terrible reneging on a promise made to Atlantic Canada, as made to other parts of the country, that a sincere effort would be made to sustain regional economic development. In fact, regional economic development has been cut throughout the country, but Atlantic Canada is suffering a great deal.
While perhaps we can accept for a moment the necessity for fiscal restraint and some pulling back, even those on the other side of the House must understand that Atlantic Canada is a particularly special case. Even now it is experiencing the prospect of a job loss of 9,000 on account of the cuts in the cod quota. Those cuts are themselves a result in large measure of the policies of the Government. Consider the fact that the cuts in quotas are attributable to decreases in the cod stock which admittedly are a result of foreign fishing, but in part perhaps due to overfishing by domestic fishermen as well. Yet we will see another 1,200 jobs cut from Summerside which already was deficient in one key role it could have been executing, to wit, the surveillance of the cod fishery to ensure that overfishing does not occur.
Even before the Budget there was the announcement of changes to the UIC which, more than any other part of the country, would affect Atlantic Canada. There were cuts in the Established Programs Financing. Perhaps 1,000 jobs will be lost as a result of events occurring over the last two months, and the Minister has the nerve and the Government has the duplicity to enter a committee meeting to try to make an announcement under conditions where it would not see the light of day that it was cutting drastically. How could a Government be so insensitive? How could a Government be so brutal in its treatment of a significant and historical part of Canada? Is it that the Government is mean? Is it that the Government is so insensitive? No, we must look for other motives. The other motive must be what has been

May 29, 1989
Supply
clear to us from the beginning, that those regional development programs like ACOA and UIC are all things the Americans do not like.
I see the Hon. Member from the Conservative Party giggling. Evidently she does not read decisions that have already been made on the American side with respect to what will be considered to be subsidies. Programs such as ACOA, DREE, DRIE, UIC, have already been cited as subsidies by the Americans in trade disputes. Let her giggle about that.
Furthermore it has been alleged that many of these programs are really not efforts to seriously affect the economic situation in the regions to which they apply. I said that the Minister came into the committee meeting two weeks ago to announce, in effect, 28 per cent cuts in ACOA. But that is only half the story. As of March 21,26 of 44 ERDAs lapsed and the Government of Nova Scotia said that only one in five would likely be renegotiated.
I do not want to get into the games that were being played by the Minister with respect to what might be negotiated between ACOA and ERDA, and changes in the relative contributions of the federal Government, but there is a most amazing consideration. My colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), said that the deficit was not mentioned before the election. There was some real activity before the election. The Government already spent $500 million of a five-year program before election day. Up until today the Government has spent $580 million.
In other words, of the $1.05 billion supposedly available to ACOA, $500 million has already been spent. When one considers that it costs $35 million a year to administer the program, there is only $200 million left until the program lapses. This would suggest that rather than an economic strategy, it was an election-winning strategy.
The House may recall that it was Mr. Savoie who pointed out that DREE, DRIE and the Atlantic Canada Development Programs all failed. He pointed out that there needed to be some means of regional economic development that would ensure the sustaining of effective economic growth in the Atlantic provinces.
However, what they received was more of the same. Let me explain. The Government sure spent money
quickly. It spent $90,000 for a company that did not exist; $54,000 for a hotel study that had already been done three times; $100,000 in market studies for four tourist developments within a few miles of one another; tens of thousands of dollars for a struggling little J.C. Irving company. Meanwhile, we are told by the author than unless there is enhancement of education and training and infrastructure, and more research and development and long-term planning with more control to the regions, it will not work. That is from the author of the report that motivated ACOA.
Members opposite should be sitting there shamefacedly over the almost deliberate failure the Government has imposed upon a program that could have been of great use to a part of this country that needs the help of Canadians generally and which should not be burdened any longer with the dominance of the core of Canada, which even today is making it more difficult. The interest rates rise not in response to the needs of Atlantic Canada but to the needs of Toronto. There has to be a stop to that, and I know you share that point of view.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak about this motion which condemns:
-the Government for initiating a series of policies that are causing unprecedented economic devastation to Atlantic Canada.
I have with me the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council report for April. It states that the Newfoundland economy is stronger than at any other time in the 1980s. Is that devastation?
It says that Prince Edward Island surprised everyone in 1988 and has had good impetus going into 1989. Is that economic devastation?
It says that Nova Scotia has one of the best records of job creation on record and its unemployment rate has dipped sharply. Is that economic devastation?
It says that New Brunswick has put together a string of good years thanks to its resource based production. While some of the bloom has now gone, newly diversified forestry production, the frigate building program and new mines offer hope for further progress. Is that economic devastation?
The report goes on to say that in APEC's eighth consecutive survey of major projects in Atlantic Canada,
May 29, 1989

there are 220 projects totalling $49 billion, up 25 per cent from the figure in 1988. Is that economic devastation?
It states further that Government plays a dominant role in the investment prospects for Atlantic Canada, accounting for two-thirds of all projects in the area by value. Is that economic devastation?
As many of my colleagues have expressed today, we have a serious fishing industry problem, a resource scarcity problem, in Atlantic Canada. That is a development that is shocking and startling and of great concern, not only to those of us in Atlantic Canada but to all the people of Canada.
Some tough decisions have been made with respect to the quotas because the intent of the Government is to manage the resource. The resource will be managed, and it will be saved.

speechtext:
With regard to the fishery, while the decisions which have been made are difficult, they are not decisions of an economic policy nature made by the Government. They are decisions of a conservation nature. They are management decisions that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) has made in terms of cutting quotas. They are political decisions that have been made in reaching agreement with France about St. Pierre and Miquelon, as my colleague from St. John's East has described them. I believe that we have to give credit to the Government and to the Minister of Fisheries for facing up to those difficult kinds of decisions.
We also face some difficult restraints and some difficult reductions in Canadian Forces Base establishments in Atlantic Canada. Those tragedies and those difficulties will be addressed. The people involved in the fishery and in the Canadian Forces Base closings will receive the help to make economic and social adjustments that will be required. I would like to return to this subject in a few moments.
Supply
I would now like to speak a bit about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which was established by this Government two years ago. This policy approach was based on the principle that lasting economic development must come largely from within the region itself, from the ideas and the initiatives of entrepreneurs and business people.
It was apparent that if the federal Government was to play a useful role in assisting business people to translate their ideas into projects that would create additional wealth for the region, then major changes were required in the structure and organization of the Government's Business Incentives Program.
The programs created by the previous Government in the early 1980s were hampered by rigid eligibility criteria, complicated application requirements, and by the fact that government support for projects over $100,000 had to be approved in Ottawa.
Just a little over a year ago, on February 15, 1988, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency introduced its Action Program. This program was tailor-made to the needs of the region's small and medium-sized business community in a number of ways, including a streamlined and simplified application program, the introduction of a progress payment to assist with bridge financing costs, and expanded coverage to important parts of the services sector. The services sector is where the majority of new business formations and employment gains are taking place.
It provided for increased support for the establishment of new business where the risks are the greatest. It provided for increased support for studies, to help business people refine business ideas and to examine ways to improve the competitiveness of their operations. It increased support for the risky and high-cost areas of innovation projects to develop new products and new services. It provided support to build up the infrastructure to support business development by making assistance available to organizations such as universities and industrial development associations to provide services to small businesses. In addition, decision-making was decentralized from Ottawa to the Atlantic region so that now over 90 per cent of all the investment decisions and applications by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency are made in the Atlantic region.

May 29, 1989
Supply
The Action Program, by its very name, promised to cut the bureaucratic red tape which was clogging the process. More than 5,200 applications have already been approved from a total of 12,000 applications received. This is more than 10 times the number of applications received under any of the old programs, and almost 15 times the number approved for implementation. The record is impressive to say the least.
Close to $600 million has been committed in the form of contributions to business investments. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, does that sound like economic devastation?
These funds will be expended over a two or three-year period as the business investment is put in place and as the government support is drawn down. Expenditures on incentives were in the order of $160 million in the past fiscal year alone. ACOA's main estimate forecast for the coming year is $280 million in financial assistance to business as a majority of the projects supported to date complete their investment plans.
How does this compare to previous Government policies? In the five-year period from 1982 to 1987, prior to the creation of ACOA, federal spending on business incentives averaged between $30 million and $35 million per year. The 1989-90 forecast of $280 million represents an eight-fold increase in historical average. The impact on the Atlantic economy of course goes beyond contributions by Government. Associated with every dollar of Government funds is close to $2 of private investment.
The Action Program has reinforced and contributed to a major resurgence of private investment in the Atlantic region, for example, capital investment was up 13 per cent in 1988. this year, the regional increase in capital investment is expected to exceed that for the country as a whole. I say to the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls (Mr. Baker) who put forward this motion, this is hardly an indication of economic devastation.
A particular objective of the Action Program is to help foster the start-up of new companies. As I have indicated, the program was designed to respond to the special needs of business.
I have had some experience in starting new businesses in the Atlantic provinces. I am pleased to say that for 30
years one of those I have started has survived the ups and downs, sometimes barely, and manages to exist still.
While financial assistance provided under the ACOA program in the past year has contributed to more than 400 people getting into business in Atlantic Canada for the first time, an idea of the impact of the program can be seen by the fact that small business formations, that is, firms with less than 50 employees, have increased by 12 per cent in the Atlantic region in 1988 as compared to 10 per cent in Canada as a whole.
The Action Program has also introduced a comprehensive and flexible program of support for the study of business planning and new innovative business ideas. As anyone familiar with the business world knows, good planning is essential to success.
Nearly 1,000 studies have been financed under the Action Program. About two-thirds of these studies were undertaken to examine the feasibility of starting a new business.
Innovation is commonly thought to be an embracing of the development of new products in the so-called growth technologies, such as microelectronics, computer software, bio-technology and advanced industrial materials. I can recite a number of cases where, with ACOA's assistance, products that are fast becoming the way of the future are already being developed in Atlantic Canada.
ACOA has also committed over $100 million in support to non-commercial organizations such as universities and business associations. I am pleased to say that in the capital city area of Fredericton close to $25 million- and I am not sure of the exact figure-has been contributed to the New Brunswick Research and Productivity Council and to the University of New Brunswick for the development of science and technology based innovative support for business and industry not just in New Brunswick but throughout Atlantic Canada.
The Fisheries Association of Newfoundland and Labrador, for example, is one indication of the kind of innovative support provided by ACOA which has received close to $1 million-$945,000 to be exact-to undertake a three-year program to promote the sale of Newfoundland capelin roe in the Japanese market.
May 29, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the changes announced recently in our action programs will largely help small and mediumsized businesses. Since the vast majority of the projects are small, 85 per cent of applications will continue to be favourably received. Projects below $200,000 will continue to qualify under the ACOA. I believe I have demonstrated that the Government's regional development policies are an unparallelled success. That success is recognized in the Atlantic Provinces, despite the rhetoric we are hearing from the other side of this House.

As I have said earlier, there is no doubt that we are facing some severe difficulties in Atlantic Canada. Those difficulties, to some extent, touch on this whole concept of sustainable development that we have heard so much about from the World Commission on Development and the Environment. What we are seeing in the fisheries is the reality of a resource that has not been as abundant as we had thought. It is not capable of supporting the industrial infrastructure we have put in place. We have come to the difficult decisions which cause us to reduce our exploitation of that resource now in favour of maintaining that resource on into the future. There is a dramatic need for support for those people and those institutions who are both economically and socially affected by this developing dilemma. I have every confidence that this Government will provide that support in those adjustment periods.
The same applies for those decisions in the name of economic restraint and fiscal responsibility which we must practice in this nation and in the concept of sustainable development which we must come to grips with. Those Canadian Forces bases closings and reductions will require major adjustment support. I have confidence that this Government will provide it.
In terms of regional development, I think that the figures speak not of economic devastation in the Atlantic region but of economic support which has been unprecedented. Five hundred million dollars is being spent in 1989 versus an average of $285 million in the previous five years and $185 million averaged in the five years before that. The average in the current five year period,
Supply
while it will drop from $500 million to perhaps $400 million one year from now and then gradually ascend, the average over the next five years will be $425 million. This is hardly a contribution to economic devastation. On the contrary, it is the commitment of this Government to economic prosperity and economic development in the Atlantic region.
It is unreasonable to claim, as one Hon. Member has claimed, that this Government's budget constitutes a rape of Atlantic Canada. That is not only unreasonable, it is irresponsible. The facts are that this Government, in a manner without precedent, has addressed economic development in the Atlantic region in very full measure. While we have to face up to a reduction in the developing thrust and in the momentum of that development, it is not by any means a return to the old days.
In terms of this Government's commitment to financial responsibility, there is one figure that has struck me, and I frequently get asked the question: "Why does the Government itself not cut its own administration? Why does restraint not begin at home?" An interesting statistic is that since this Government took office in 1984, the Public Service has been reduced by 11,000 person-years. The Public Service today is the same size that it was in 1973. I wonder how many businesses in Canada could make that kind of a claim in terms of keeping their own house in order.
There are four things that I would like to say briefly that we must do in Atlantic Canada, and in fact in Canada. First, all Canadians, including Atlantic Canadians must recognize the deeply serious debt dilemma in which our country finds itself. Unless we demonstrate the financial responsibility, strength and courage to deal with that debt, to get it down, to alleviate the constant interest growth and the constant interest component of our spending, we will not be able to deal with any special problems, let alone address development in places like the Atlantic region, as we have. Second, we must accept and support the restraint measures. I believe that Canadians do accept and support the restraint measures that this Government is practising. I know it is difficult for all of us to see a service like VIA Rail diminished or in prospect be diminished. I hope that the operators of VIA Rail will find a way to maintain a large part of that

May 29, 1989
Supply
service, and to find innovative and exciting ways to serve Canadians with it.
The figures are absolutely staggering. VIA Rail is such an expensive service and program that it conflicts with the very possibility of developing such major infrastructure projects so central to the development of Atlantic Canada. For example, the Trans-Canada Highway system in New Brunswick. Therefore, to face up to the cost of VIA Rail, to measure the fact that it serves only 5 per cent or less of the transportation market, to recognize that it has consumed $3 billion in subsidies over the past eight years while its ridership has diminished, is only to be financially responsible.
Third, we must emphasize the priorities for which Atlantic Canadians are famous. We must exercise priorities toward entrepreneurship which ACOA has done, toward the export on a free trade basis of our services, such as engineering, to the development of our forest industry, to aquaculture, to mining and to the attraction to Atlantic Canada of viable new industries. Atlantic Canada is a great place to live, work and to build a career.
Fourth, we must, and I believe that this Government will, establish those support programs, that adjustment assistance for those distressed situations that I have described, in the fishery, in the Canadian Forces base reductions.
I would like to tell the people of Atlantic Canada that they are well represented in this Government. We are 12 strong on this side of the House from Atlantic Canada. The message for Atlantic Canada does get delivered. The response will be forthcoming. The Throne Speech set out a mission for all of Canada. In four parts it talked of economic growth, of the environmental imperative, of a caring and compassionate society, and of a unified and distinctive Canadian identity. In many ways, Atlantic Canada will measure up to that Throne Speech challenge as a model.
In closing, I would like to make one more point about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and to draw the parallel to the motion about economic devastation. Donald Savoie, the developer, or at least the author of many of the principles of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency has been quoted several times today in context and out of context.
He credits the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency with avoiding the pitfalls of previous regional economic programs that poured hundreds and millions of dollars into white elephants, such as heavy water plants and importing outside industries that collapsed when the grants dried up. He said rather that "75 per cent of ACOA's money has gone to locally based ventures valued at less than $200,000 and 90 per cent has gone to aid projects of less than $1 million." He said that: "they have done"-and he is referring to the Government-"an excellent job in building up credibility with local entrepreneurs, so I think the question should not be whether ACOA spends the remaining half a billion dollars in three years or five years, but how it spends the remaining money." That remaining money is going to be well spent developing entrepreneurs, developing economic prosperity in the Atlantic region. I undertake, and my colleagues from Atlantic Canada and this Government undertake to ensure that that does happen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if all of those emotional and dramatic analogies were absolutely accurate, it would not be fair. It is unfortunate that this Government has had to take the financially responsible steps of addressing itself to the deficit and interest cost problems and has had to restrain the momentum of its activities in many ways. It is also unfortunate that we cannot continue to be all things to all people such as in the retention of a VIA
May 29, 1989

Rail system that less than 5 per cent of the population of this country uses. My understanding from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) is that the nine protected routes represent isolated communities to which there is no other means of travel. Is it fair that the 95 per cent or 98 per cent of the people of New Brunswick who use the TransCanada Highway system should be denied its rebuilding or imperilled in its use for years because we spend half a billion dollars each year in subsidies to maintain a passenger rail service that less than 5 per cent of the population uses. I do not think that is fair.
In so far as freight transport rates are concerned, I have spoken in this House in the past two weeks about the retention of freight rail service to the Saint John River valley. If it is viable on analysis, then I would certainly fight for it to be retained. I have spoken extensively about the impact of ACOA this afternoon. ACOA has created immense economic activity in Atlantic Canada which will be reflected over the next two or three years when the money now committed is drawn down and the projects are started.
